items.title: Researchers say AI agents have a 'half-life' where their success rate declines exponentially with task length, causing multi-step workflows to fail more often [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: AI Agents have a half-life
items.summary:
Researchers describe AI agents as having a 'half-life,' meaning their probability of successfully completing tasks decreases exponentially with task duration due to a constant failure rate per unit time. This explains why agents with high per-step accuracy still fail frequently on longer, multi-step jobs, as the cumulative chance of failure grows with each additional step.

The concept challenges the assumption that longer tasks fail due to increased complexity or ambiguity, instead attributing failures to exposure time. For example, a 95% accurate agent completing a 48-step workflow may succeed only about 8.5% of the time. While model improvements have extended agents' effective task duration over time, many real-world applications still face reliability issues, leading to project cancellations. Reducing task length or exposure is suggested as a more immediate solution than waiting for better models.

items.title: Study audits AI restaurant and bar recommendations against a complete census of 4,776 venues in Bali, finding 85.6% never recommended and frequent staleness issues [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Invisible to the Machine: auditing AI recommendation against a complete census
items.summary: A study evaluated AI recommendation systems including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Perplexity by comparing their suggestions against a full census of 4,776 cafes, restaurants, and bars in two Bali markets. It found that 85.6% of venues were never recommended by any system, including 72.6% of well-established venues, and that recommendations were influenced by factors like review volume and website presence rather than star ratings. The study also observed low agreement between systems and frequent recommendations of permanently closed venues, indicating staleness rather than hallucination as a common failure mode.

items.originalTitle: Ownership in the Age of AI
items.summary:
A new blog post by a tech lead highlights the importance of ownership in software development as AI-generated code becomes more common. The author argues that while AI should be used aggressively to handle routine coding tasks, engineers must be able to defend every decision in their code without relying on AI tools for explanations. This approach ensures accountability and preserves the value of human judgment in complex systems.

The post warns that outsourcing understanding to AI risks creating fragile codebases and slows team productivity by shifting the cognitive load to reviewers. It also cautions against mistaking AI-generated sophistication for true expertise, emphasizing that engineers should build mental models of their systems through active engagement rather than passive acceptance of AI outputs. The author advises against posting AI-generated text directly in team communications, as it can undermine trust and clarity.

items.originalTitle: What happens when an LLM never sees material beyond fifth grade?
items.summary:
Researchers developed LittleLearner, a large language model trained solely on an 88-billion-token corpus filtered to US Common Core standards for grades K–5, to investigate how limiting training data complexity affects model capabilities. The study compares models trained on this restricted curriculum with unfiltered controls to understand the impact on language understanding and reasoning beyond fifth-grade material.

Experiments show that scaling model size, post-training fine-tuning, and in-context learning improve performance within the K–5 scope but do not enhance abilities on tasks requiring knowledge beyond that level. This controlled setup allows researchers to attribute capability gains directly to training data exposure and explore questions about learning efficiency, concept acquisition, and comparisons between machine and child learners.

items.originalTitle: AWS Open-Sources Dogwood, Extending Cedar to Govern Sequences of Agent Tool Calls
items.summary:
AWS has released Dogwood as an open-source policy language that extends Cedar by adding temporal conditions to evaluate sequences of agent tool calls rather than individual requests. This allows policies to govern approvals, rate limits, and cumulative actions based on an agent's event history. Dogwood is supported within AgentCore Policy but its reference interpreter is intended for testing, not production use.

Dogwood introduces temporal operators that analyze event histories, enabling policies to enforce constraints like approval before action or limits on cumulative interactions. While existing Cedar policies remain valid, Dogwood requires stateful event tracking and does not support Cedar's automated reasoning tools. AWS highlights challenges such as concurrency effects on policy enforcement and the need for trusted event logs and secure data retention to ensure policy effectiveness.

Early users have applied Optima to finance, legal writing, and image recognition tasks to identify models that balance cost and performance effectively.

Techniques like Google’s SynthID-Text and Meta’s TextSeal modify the randomness in token selection without compromising the model’s capabilities or user privacy.

Critics’ concerns about reduced writing quality stem from misunderstandings of how watermarking interacts with model randomness. Additionally, AI-generated text has long exhibited identifiable stylistic patterns, making watermarking a formalized but not revolutionary step in AI content detection.

items.title: ShieldFont uses ligature-based text substitutions to disrupt AI scrapers that ignore robots.txt, rendering scraped content nonsensical while appearing normal to users [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ShieldFont: Bludgeoning AI Scrapers That Disrespect Robots.txt
items.summary:
ShieldFont is a new method designed to combat AI scrapers that disregard robots.txt files by substituting about a quarter of words with ligature-based versions. These substitutions cause scraped HTML text to appear grammatically valid but nonsensical, while the rendered font looks normal to human readers. This approach aims to protect static or archived content marked as 'do not follow' from unauthorized scraping.

The technique has drawbacks, such as affecting screen readers and legitimate search engine bots, and advanced scrapers could bypass it by parsing rendered text, though this increases scraping costs. ShieldFont complements other anti-scraping tools like maze traps and dynamic content generation to make scraping more difficult and resource-intensive for AI systems.
